summary: Workshop on establishing apples-to-apples benchmark methodology for runtime performance across hosted/dedicated/private deployments. Covered prompt set design, warm vs cold cache, continuous batching, KV cache priming, quantized model parity, network overhead (VPC/on-prem), and load generation best practices. Agreed on next steps to exchange harness, prompt sets, and provision Aurora staging for baseline runs.
transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2025-06-10 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~78 minutes
Attendees: Ethan Park (Redwood AE), Maya Rodriguez (Redwood SE), Liam Chen (Aurora CTO), Aisha Khan (Aurora Lead ML Eng), Oliver Brooks (Aurora Infra), Sophie Patel (Aurora PM)

Summary (auto): align on benchmark methodology for runtime and deployment variants; capture assumptions; agree baseline tests.

00:00 - Ethan Park: hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro, we want to make sure when we compare hosted vs dedicated vs your on-prem setup it's apples to apples. maya will drive the methodology.
00:26 - Maya Rodriguez: cool, hi all. real quick: goal is twofold - latency SLO analysis and throughput cost tradeoffs. we'll cover prompt sets, load generation, caching behaviors (kv cache), batching, and quantization parity. any immediate constraints?
00:45 - Liam Chen: timeline is tight, we want initial baselines within two weeks, and then a pilot. also important: VPC traffic will go through our firewall, so network adds latency.
01:05 - Aisha Khan: our production prompts vary a lot, short form payments messages and longer compliance summaries. token lengths average 45 tokens but tail to 600 in some cases.
01:28 - Maya Rodriguez: perfect, that's critical. for apples-to-apples we'll ask for distribution: p50/p90/p99 token lengths. also need examples of deterministic prompts vs stochastic sampling config.
01:50 - Oliver Brooks: on infra, we have a private cloud with limited GPU capacity; we can spin up an isolated subnet for testing. want keep data in VPC.
02:10 - Ethan Park: thanks. quick agenda - methodology principles, prompt set construction, load generation patterns, caching & batching experiments, quantization checks, and measurement/reporting.
02:34 - Maya Rodriguez: principle 1: define the user-perceived latency point - is it end-to-end from client request to first token, full response, or token streaming? we recommend both p50/p95 for first token and p99 for full response.
02:58 - Sophie Patel: for our product, first token is critical for UI perceived latency, full response matters for batch reconciliation jobs.
03:18 - Maya Rodriguez: OK we'll collect both. principle 2: control for model config - sampling temperature, top_k/top_p, max_tokens, and consider greedy vs sampling. quantization should match the model weights used in prod.
03:45 - Aisha Khan: on quantization, we've seen differences in hallucination and latency between 8-bit and 4-bit. how do we ensure parity?
04:05 - Maya Rodriguez: good question. methodology: run functional equivalence checks on a validation prompt set before perf runs - compare logits / token distributions where possible, or at least output quality metrics (BLEU/ROUGE-ish or human eval) to ensure quantized variant isn't degrading outputs beyond an acceptability threshold.
04:34 - Liam Chen: will that add time to the benchmark? we need a fast path.
04:44 - Maya Rodriguez: yes, so two-stage: 1) quick smoke quality checks on 200 prompts, 2) full perf runs. if 4-bit shows significant drift, flag it and run both 8-bit and 4-bit to show cost/quality tradeoff.
05:05 - Ethan Park: next, prompt sets. we recommend 3 sets: "short interactive" (~<64 tokens), "mixed" (p50~45, p90~300), and "long batch" (>300 tokens). send us a sample of 200 for each.
05:28 - Aisha Khan: we'll extract from prod logs and sanitize PII. expect to share by tomorrow.
05:38 - Maya Rodriguez: excellent. tokenization note: ensure you use the same tokenizer/version and pre-tokenize in the harness; differences can skew tokens/sec metrics. also include explicit sequence length histogram.
06:05 - Oliver Brooks: for VPC/on-prem, do you measure just server-side runtime or include NAT/firewall hops?
06:20 - Maya Rodriguez: we capture both. baseline includes server-side compute-only (measured locally on host), and end-to-end which includes network RTT and client overhead. we'll report both so you can see network impact.
06:40 - Liam Chen: how do you handle warm vs cold cache? our users have large prefix reuse so KV cache matters.
06:50 - Maya Rodriguez: two experiments: cold-start (empty KV, model cold), and warm (preload KV cache by replaying a representative set). for continuous services, also measure steady-state after sustained QPS to capture batching behavior.
07:12 - Ethan Park: for KV cache priming we'll provide a priming script: replay 10k historical sessions to populate prefix caches. note that some runtimes evict caches over time, so specify eviction policy.
07:36 - Aisha Khan: eviction is LRU with a 4GB cap on our nodes.
07:45 - Maya Rodriguez: documented. important to record memory footprint and KV hit rate; we'll instrument to log hit/miss ratios.
08:00 - Sophie Patel: on batching, what batch sizes are realistic?
08:08 - Maya Rodriguez: depends on latency target. for sub-200ms p50 you likely need small batches (1-4). for highest throughput runs measure with larger batching to see tokens/sec improvements. we recommend sweeping batch sizes [1,4,8,16,32] and recording latency percentiles and throughput.
08:34 - Liam Chen: will we test dynamic batching or static?
08:38 - Maya Rodriguez: both. dynamic continuous batching that groups in-flight requests will be more realistic; static batch runs (fixed batch sizes) help isolate kernel efficiency.
08:52 - Ethan Park: a note on measurement - include wall-clock time per request, server-side compute time, kernel-level counters if available, and GPU utilization. GPU metrics help explain tail latency due to congestion.
09:10 - Oliver Brooks: for on-prem we can enable NVIDIA perf counters and nsys traces for a subset of runs.
09:18 - Maya Rodriguez: great - those traces are useful. we only need a couple for deep-dive.
09:25 - Aisha Khan: load generation - how do you emulate production concurrency?
09:34 - Maya Rodriguez: use a traffic-replay approach with arrival process matching your production (we ask for inter-arrival distribution), plus Poisson bursts to stress tails. run incremental QPS ramp (10%,25%,50%,75%,100% of target), each step for 5-10 minutes to get steady-state.
09:58 - Sophie Patel: what's your recommended run length to get stable p99?
10:05 - Maya Rodriguez: at least 5 minutes per step for p95, 10-15 minutes per step for robust p99 estimates. total run time can be a few hours; we'll plan accordingly.
10:22 - Ethan Park: on metric normalization - report tokens/sec, requests/sec, p50/p95/p99 latency (first token & full response), cost per 1M tokens estimate, and KV cache hit rate.
10:42 - Liam Chen: cost per 1M tokens depends on reserved vs on-demand pricing; we'll model both.
10:50 - Maya Rodriguez: yes. for dedicated we estimate using your committed pricing; for hosted we use Redwood published rates and include egress if applicable.
11:03 - Aisha Khan: quantization parity again - will you provide a reproducible build? we want to run the same quantized weights on our infra.
11:12 - Maya Rodriguez: yes, we'll provide the quantization pipeline and a docker image that reproduces the same kernels. for 4-bit we usually use Q4-type libs; we'll pin versions.
11:26 - Liam Chen: any pitfalls with tokenizer differences across runtimes?
11:33 - Maya Rodriguez: tokenizers vary; always pre-tokenize with the same tokenizer implementation and version. also for benchmarks make sure you measure tokens generated by model, not characters.
11:46 - Oliver Brooks: network noise in our VPC sometimes causes spiky p99s; should we run multiple trials?
11:53 - Maya Rodriguez: exactly - run at least three independent trials and report median curves; include variance. we'll also capture system logs to correlate spikes with network events.
12:10 - Ethan Park: instrumentation: we'll add request IDs and attach traces to correlate client request to server timeline. that helps root-cause p99s.
12:24 - Sophie Patel: what about reproducibility for sampling randomness?
12:30 - Maya Rodriguez: run with fixed seeds for deterministic runs; for stochastic testing run multiple seeds and report averaged metrics. note that sampling affects token counts and hence latency, so include both greedy and sampling configs.
12:52 - Aisha Khan: what about evaluation for output quality vs perf? we need to show tradeoffs.
13:00 - Maya Rodriguez: include an eval harness: run n=1k sample prompts and score against reference metrics (if available), and also capture human-eval markers for drift. plot quality vs cost heatmap.
13:20 - Liam Chen: okay, in terms of artifacts you will deliver?
13:26 - Maya Rodriguez: 1) benchmark harness repo + docker image, 2) load generation scripts and example workload configs, 3) baseline report template (latency, throughput, cost), 4) priming and warm-up scripts, 5) kernel traces and recommended debug commands.
13:48 - Ethan Park: we'll also include a short doc on how to provision a VPC test cluster and Redwood's security checklist for private deployments.
14:00 - Sophie Patel: great. can we also get a short checklist for what to sanitize in prompt sets?
14:07 - Maya Rodriguez: yes - remove PII, redact account ids, remove user identifiers, replace with placeholders, and include a mapping doc for anonymization so we can interpret results.
14:20 - Aisha Khan: about the apples-to-apples comparison - do you recommend freezing model code and runtime versions?
14:30 - Maya Rodriguez: absolutely. freeze model weights, tokenizer, runtime binaries (cuda/cudnn/torch/transformer lib versions), and quantization libs. capture software versions in your run metadata so comparisons are valid.
14:55 - Oliver Brooks: in our environment we have slightly older GPU drivers; will that break things?
15:02 - Maya Rodriguez: it can change kernel selection and perf. we can run a compatibility check and flag differences. if necessary, we can provide a recommended driver set or note the delta in the report.
15:20 - Ethan Park: ok final section: reporting and visualization. we'll provide a dashboard with latency curves, tokens/sec, KV hit rates, and cost projections.
15:34 - Liam Chen: can you include sample raw CSV exports?
15:39 - Maya Rodriguez: yes - raw logs for the team.
15:45 - Sophie Patel: next steps recap?
15:48 - Ethan Park: recap: Maya to share harness + docker (due 6/13), Aurora to share prompt sets & tokenization notes (due 6/12), Oliver to provision VPC test environment (due 6/16), Ethan to send pricing/pilot template (due 6/11). schedule follow-up week of 6/20 to review results.
16:10 - Aisha Khan: sounds good. any other questions?
16:15 - Liam Chen: curious: will you include model fallback behavior under heavy load?
16:20 - Maya Rodriguez: yes - we'll test routing policies: fallback to smaller model or increased batching when SLOs can't be met; include functional tests to validate no silent failures.
16:36 - Oliver Brooks: thanks, we'll coordinate infra access with Ethan.
16:40 - Ethan Park: thanks all. we'll send meeting notes and artifacts after this call.
16:48 - [end]
